Hi Jules —

Quick one as we prep the next pilot invoice: BrightCart’s integration shows a lot of long histories per end-user (multi-turn carts, order history, product browsing). Before we push the trial into production, the procurement team asked a couple of specific billing questions we want to make sure are answered in writing. TL;DR: how does compacting (trimming + summary-ing prior turns) impact billed tokens, and how do rounding/minimums apply across streaming vs non-streamed calls?

Two specific examples in plain language would help:
1) User A sends a 120-token prompt with a trimmed history that ends up as 800 tokens after compaction. Do we bill 800 tokens or the full original 5,200 tokens stored elsewhere?
2) For long streaming responses where we flush partial tokens every 30s, how does the quantum/rounding apply (per-chunk vs per-session)?

I attached a short exhibit with three invoice-line examples (billing-exhibit-v2.pdf) — would you take a look and tell me which lines are confusing from your side? If procurement wants a written concession, flag it so I can loop in legal and pricing.

Thanks — would love to close these last operational questions so Finance can sign-off on the pilot.

Jules — thanks, good questions. Quick answers up front: we bill based on the tokenized request that the runtime executes after any server-side compaction/normalization steps. In practice that means the post-compaction token count is the primary billed unit. A few important nuances follow in the attached exhibit; I’m pasting two example lines here for clarity.

Example A — single non-streaming call (hosted):
- Original stored history: 5,200 tokens (raw)
- Server-side compaction run -> produced compacted prompt: 800 tokens
- Response tokens (generated): 420 tokens
- Billed tokens = 800 (prompt, post-compaction) + 420 (response) = 1,220 tokens
- Rounding quantum (hosted API) = 250-token slabs -> billed slab = 1,250 tokens

Example B — streaming response flushed every 30s (hosted):
- Each flush is charged at the moment it’s emitted using the runtime’s observed token counts for prompt + incremental generation since last flush
- We apply the same 250-token quantum to the total session bill, not per-flush, to avoid compounding rounding on typical streaming patterns. So even if we flush four times, we sum tokens first then round once at the end of the session.

Key differentiator: for Dedicated (reserved) pools where you purchase committed throughput, the quantum is larger (1,000-token slabs) and we apply committed-offset accounting before rounding. That reduces rounding overhead for high-volume flows.

I attached the updated exhibit with the arithmetic lines showing pre-compaction, post-compaction, response, quantum, and final billed slabs. If you want, I can export the same examples into CSV so you can plug into your forecasting model.

Regarding the requested 20% retroactive credit for the first three months: we don’t standardly do retroactive overage credits at that level, but we can offer a controlled pilot concession. Camila — can you propose an operational pilot concession that preserves unit economics but addresses BrightCart’s risk?

— Ben

Thanks — adding a little more color from pricing/ops side so procurement has concrete language. Two new operational constructs we can offer for the pilot: 

1) Compact Context Credit (CCC) pilot (90 days) — we quantify the tokens saved by Redwood’s server-side compaction vs your raw stored history and apply a credit equal to 25% of the "tokens saved" line-item, capped at 100k saved tokens per month. This credit shows on the invoice as a negative line-item ("CCC pilot: tokens-saved credit").

2) Metering grace and rounding policy — for hosted customers we round final session totals to the nearest 250-token slab. To prevent microburst inefficiency from small heartbeats we compute streaming sessions as a single session-level aggregation and round once per session. For Dedicated customers we round to 1,000 tokens. If you opt into dedicated reserved capacity we can also provide a per-month rounding amortization (carry-forward of fractional slabs) for high-volume months.

Note about cache/prefix reuse: if a prefix is served from KV cache and is not re-encoded at request time, we apply a prefix-reuse credit (negative token adjustment) up to the limit of the pilot rules. That means repeated identical system prompts don't generate full prompt token charges repeatedly — only the new tokens and the delta are counted.

Operational ask: If BrightCart wants the CCC pilot, we’ll need two items in the SOW: (a) definition of the compaction algorithm (we’ll include a deterministic summary pipeline) and (b) acceptance metrics for the 90-day trial (monthly reporting cadence; if >70% of compaction edits change user-visible behavior we’ll pause credits pending re-eval).

I’m attaching the CSV with the line-by-line math so you can drop it into your forecast.

Cheers,

- CCC pilot (90 days): we will apply the token-saved credit in the invoice month the savings are measured (no delayed bookkeeping).
- Overages: instead of a 20% retroactive credit, Redwood can commit to a 10% overage credit on above-forecast metered tokens for months 1–3.
- Liability cap: we can agree to a $7,500/month cap during the pilot window. If BrightCart hits the cap two months in a row, we’ll schedule a joint ops review and pause automatic credits until remediation steps are defined.
